question: The ferro-alloy and silicon metal industry plays a key role in European value chains in connection with the production of steel, aluminium, batteries and semiconductors, and also in relation to energy technologies and the defence sector. At the same time, however, the sector is under heavy import pressure, primarily from China.

A matter of particular concern is the fact that silicon metal, which has been recognised by the European Union as a strategic and critical raw material, has not been granted protection of the sort accorded to certain ferroalloys. As a result, EU production has been virtually eliminated. Silicon metal is increasingly being used as a substitute for ferro-silicon in certain industrial applications.

The silicon metal currently being imported – primarily from China and Angola – is placed on the EU market at such low prices that industrial users use it in preference to ferro-silicon. This undermines the effectiveness of the entire safeguard mechanism in place for ferro-alloy production.
In view of the deteriorating situation of the European ferro-alloy and silicon metal industry, I would like to put the following questions to the European Commission: 1.
Has the European Commission analysed the phenomenon whereby silicon metal is used as a substitute for ferro-silicon, rendering ineffective the safeguards put in place for ferro-silicon?
How does the Commission intend to take into consideration the status of silicon metal as a strategic and critical raw material when developing the EU’s industrial and commercial policy?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The European Commission has imposed definitive safeguard measures on imports of certain ferroalloys into the EU on 18 November 2025. A comparison of import data of January to April 2025 with January to April 2026 shows a decrease of import volumes and fluctuating import prices.

In order to thoroughly analyse the effectiveness of the measure, the Commission will initiate a review no later than November 2026. As regards silicon metal, there are anti-dumping measures in place on imports from China since 1990, which have been continued following several reviews which have extended the measures before they expired.

The Commission is committed to ensuring the effectiveness of measures in place and may initiate a review to reexamine the measures where there is evidence to suggest that they may no longer be sufficient to counteract the negative effects of dumped imports. The Commission engages with the EU industry requesting to review the existing measures to ensure that the correct evidentiary standards are met.

If these standards are met, an investigation is initiated to examine the circumstances with a view to adapting the measures if necessary. The Commission considers carefully the designation of strategic and critical raw materials when developing commercial and industrial policies.
Relatedly, promoting the recycling of strategic and critical raw materials in general in the EU is also of important consideration in these.
